title: The Stories of Awakening
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Keizan Zenji's picture of Buddha sitting six years until reeds grow through the mat, and sets beside it case 41, Bodhidharma's nine years facing a wall. A poem about falling into the same hole in the sidewalk leads Nomon to ask whether the habitual "me" can appreciate such heroic stories at all. Bodhidharma answers the emperor with "no merit" and "vast emptiness," then Huike and Sengcan each search for a mind or a wrongdoing and cannot find it. Nomon closes with verses from Sengcan's Faith in Mind and describes the night's yaza, a bell-free sitting where people drift in, walk, or sleep.

sentences.text: This poem reminds me a little bit of practicing sesshin.
Autobiography in five chapters.
There's someone named Nyoshul Khenpo.
*Chapter 1.
I walk down the street.
There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.
I fall in.
I am lost.
I am hopeless.
It isn't my fault.
It takes forever to find a way out.*
*Chapter 2.
I walk down the same street.
There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.
I pretend I don't see it.
I fall in again.
I can't believe I'm in the same place.
But it isn't my fault.
It still takes a long time to get out.*
*Chapter 3.
I walk down the same street.
There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.
I see it is there.
I still fall in.
It's a habit.
My eyes are open.
I know where I am.
It is my fault.
I get out immediately.*
*Chapter 4.
I walk down the same street.
There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.
I walk around it.*
*Chapter 5.
I walk down another street.*
Chuckles.
It's pretty funny, isn't it?
Watching your own mind for a day or two.
Having the sort of luxury of some distractions so you don't notice that you're falling in the same hole.
And you think it's not your fault.
I just want to appreciate again, echoing Jeff's words yesterday, how wonderful it is that we get to do this sesshin together.
It's a sort of quiet big step.
And I hope we're not falling into too many holes, for both the Seattle and the Bellingham Zen Sanghas.
In Bellingham it's the first time we've had a multi-day sesshin without Norman Fischer here.
So it's kind of like, daddy's not here.
Laughter.
But we're doing okay.
Laughter.
And he sends his blessings, by the way.
And he'll talk to daddy.
Laughter.
So that's wonderful.
And of course it's the first time we've had a combined sesshin with the Seattle group, and it's so wonderful to get to make new Dharma friends.
I really agree with what Jeff was saying.
There really is nothing like sesshin, and it has so many aspects.
One of my favorites is getting to know people without any of the usual sort of social stuff going on.
So now I have a dozen new friends.
I hardly know their names.
I don't know what their jobs are, or what little things they're going to say that are wonderful or annoying or anything like that.
I just know that they're wonderful human beings who must live somewhere near Seattle.
Laughter.
Probably.
And they appear to all be very worthy Zen practitioners, very devoted to Dharma.
They have a lot of silence to practice.
So that's wonderful.
So welcome.
Welcome again.
People that might be from Seattle, I don't really know.
And then I also want to appreciate the stalwart Bellingham students who just show up to these things and really make it work.
So especially Karen and Marty and Kate and Talus and Terry, who year after year, we just keep doing this.
And each year it gets a little smoother.
I don't know if it gets any easier.
I have trouble with this particular talk.
We've had some sort of Rohatsu sesshin for a dozen years maybe, or eight or ten maybe.
At first it was an evening, and then it was half a day, and then it was a day, and now it's this, right?
So who knows what will happen next week or next year.
And I always feel like, well, it's a sesshin honoring Buddha.
And so we should tell Buddha's story and celebrate Buddha and think about Buddha, and we should in some way sort of be worthy of Buddha.

And then if you talk about or think about the story of Buddha, as Jeff was saying yesterday, it's such a sort of impossibly heroic story that in some way it activates in most of us, I think, a sort of deep sense of unworthiness.
I barely get through the day with 20 people helping me.
Jeff shared with us Keizan Zenji's wonderful homage to Buddha yesterday, so let me read that again.
So Keizan Zenji: in Soto Zen they say there are two founders, and all Zen history is quite revisionist and tidied up, so it wasn't really this way, but they say there are two founders.
Dogen is the first founder, and he's kind of the Dharma philosopher of Soto Zen.
Deep, wonderful works of pure expression of Dharma.
But when he died, there were only a couple of dozen people that ever heard of Dogen, and they probably hadn't even invented the word Soto Zen.
So in a way, at the time he wasn't that important.
It's in retrospect he became very important.
So he's the first founder, and then the second founder is Keizan Joken, who was two generations later, and he's kind of the storyteller of Soto Zen.
His masterwork is essentially a big long storybook about all the different ancestors in the lineage.
And he's also credited with popularizing Soto Zen, which also isn't quite true.
It turns out he had some really great descendants who did that, but that's okay.
They're probably glad to give him credit.
And so his masterwork, I could say, is this sort of storybook about the ancestors.
He had access to a lot of Song dynasty Chinese sources, some of which were brought back literally by Dogen in a backpack.
They had a wonderful library at Eiheiji, I guess, when Keizan was alive.
It burned down not too long after that.

So he knew some stuff of what happened according to what some people in China had written down 50 to 200 years before, and they were writing about people before them, so who knows what really happened.
But in a way it doesn't matter, because religion is an archetypal story-generating business.
It can sort of stand next to historical reality in a way that there's not really a conflict unless we need there to be.
So who knows whether Keizan's stories have any sort of historical accuracy, but they're great stories.
Then our question this morning is how can we appreciate these stories in a way that is helpful and supportive of our practice of walking down the street and falling into that damn hole again.
But here again is what Keizan said about Buddha.
*That he left home* soft peddling the problems with abandoning his wife and child.
That's another story.
*He left home and he sat on an indestructible seat so immobile that there were cobwebs in his brows, a bird's nest on his head, and reeds growing up through his mat.* So he's outside.
*Thus he sat for six years until suddenly enlightened when the morning star appeared.
And then he made the statement: I and all beings on earth together attain enlightenment at the same time.*
So how does one respond to such a story?
It's obviously a myth.
We don't think a human being could sit still for six years.
But it implies a powerful devotion, a singular vision of practice, a dropping away of doubt and confusion, a steadiness.
Does that inspire us?
Does it amuse us a little bit?
Does it intimidate us?
How does your indestructible seat feel right now?
So we had, I think it was a week ago, a memorial service for a member named Mark Livingston.
We were marking one year since he died.
It was wonderful to be able to offer that space and support to his family, and a few of us students were here too.
In the funeral, which was a year before, the people spoke to each other.
The speakers were up in front and they spoke to the audience.
Mark had just died.
His ashes were there.
But in the memorial ceremony we turned it around.
His ashes were still here, I guess they haven't had a chance to scatter them.
But we turned it around and we talked to Mark as if Mark were here.
He was a big, gentle, lovely man, very humble, quiet, liked to work.
When you walk in the front door there's a concrete ramp you probably didn't notice.
But when we got the building there was a little step up, and because of ADA requirements we were required to make a ramp.
He made that ramp out of concrete.
He did lots of other work.
So is he still here because of his ramp and his shelves, the shelves in the library that he painted, and that he always sat on a seat right about there?
Or is he gone, never to be back again?
I think culturally we come to this practice with a pretty narrow view of time.
My wife and I moved to Bellingham 20 years ago this year, and most everyone that I know is like a transplant in Bellingham.
So that's one of the things that you talk about with other transplanted Bellinghamsters, who say, oh, when did you move down?
It's just a common topic, and they say, oh, 4 or 5 years ago, and you say, oh, I moved here 20 years ago.
They say, oh, you're impressed.
You've done something good.
They stay put for 20 years.
In Japan last summer we got to stay in a temple for a week, living in a temple which is a newer temple, it was only 500 years old.

As soon as we arrived we went to the Abbot's Graveyard in the back of the temple, where they have a sort of stupa-shaped stone marker for each of the abbots for those 500 years, including Suzuki Roshi, it was his temple.
We were there with his son and his grandson, and we offered incense.

Somehow you could sort of feel that that incense smoke was the same smoke, or mingling with the smoke of 500 years of offering incense on that site, and there was a beautiful sense of reverence and love.
Even though we also knew that Suzuki Roshi's son, Suzuki Hoitsu, who was officiating at the ceremony, is now mid-70s.
He had a really hard childhood.
He did not appreciate his father very much.
His father was not there for him, his father was focused on other things.
I don't know that his father was abusive, but certainly neglectful.

And his grandson had never met Suzuki Shunryu, but you could just see in their bodies and hear in their chanting that they were deeply honoring Suzuki Roshi and all the other 500 abbots of Rinso-in Temple.
I know if you have the good fortune in our area to have a positive connection with native people here, it's the same kind of feeling.
Their people came to Bellingham 8,000 years ago, 10,000 years ago, and there's that same feeling of some kind of connection that you can't really exactly talk about.
They use words like ancestors, and they have ritual ways of remembering the ancestors, just like we're doing now.
But it seems like it's not helpful for me to remember Buddha.

Jeff talked quite eloquently yesterday about how in sesshin practice you can kind of watch as the inputs and thoughts and impulses and sensations get so quickly woven together into some sort of something that we call identity.
I was thinking later that maybe even that word identity is a little problematic, because it's a noun.
It makes it sound like there's some something.
Where do we think it is?
Like in our head?
Where is this identity, something that exists?
Maybe what we call identity is more like a habit or a process or a tendency to respond to the events in our life in a certain way and weave them together in a certain way that we call me.

So it could be that this me who likes this and doesn't like that, and wishes people would be more like that and less like this, and likes you, except when you do that, that me, who is by necessity and design bound up in a certain sort of process, maybe that me can't actually appreciate Buddha.
Maybe that me, when he hears about the reeds growing up through the mat for six years, doesn't have anywhere to go with that.
There are a few obvious ways to go, right?
One is: you should have seen that terrible thought I had, it's embarrassing.
I think that would happen if we verbalized all the thoughts in the meditation hall.
We could try that sometime.
That me is not the right me.
Maybe I'm starting from the wrong seat when that me is operant.
So is there another me that's somehow beyond the me that's bound up in that way?
And who is that?
Where do I find him or her, or does that person even have gender?

For some reason, earlier when Jeff and I were trying to explore this topic, and it's so fun to get to work with Jeff, because it took about ten minutes of conversation to plan this whole sesshin, literally.
One email, and I run into him in the hallway and I'm meeting about something else, and he says, what should we talk about for sesshin?
I said, okay, great.
And anyway, somehow we were talking about working with the heroic story of Buddha, and is there a way we can work with that that's more helpful?
Somehow the fragment of this case 41 just popped into my mind.
At the time I didn't actually remember the beginning of the case, which Jeff deliberately spared you of yesterday.
So now I'm going to subject you to the whole thing, because it's another Zen story of super macho heroic practice.
So how do we work with this?
But this is our lineage.
This is our ancestry.
This strong way of looking at practice and life.
You might have noticed it's a little bit challenging to sit still from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.
I'm sorry to tell you that's a pretty light-duty sesshin schedule.
It gets much worse if you want it to be.
So how do we work with these stories?
Jeff mentioned this part where Bodhidharma, who's kind of like the Zen Buddha, has exactly the same story more or less as the Buddha: just a hardcore practitioner on his own.
That's an important part of the story.
You know the Buddha story, that he worked with different teachers and sort of quickly mastered whatever they had to teach him.

He ended up with a couple of buddies and they did a bunch of practice together, very hardcore austere practice, and finally he left even them because he felt like, that's not quite it, I need to do this my own way.
So Bodhidharma, the same way.
Somehow an Indian monk traveled an unbelievable long journey to China on his own.
I think they never say to Bodhidharma, do you have any friends?
Do you have parents?
We don't know, because he's kind of an archetypal character.
They now think that there probably was a physical person, but that was not agreed upon for a while.
It was leaning the other way for a while, that it was purely a myth.
It seems like it's leaning the other way back.
So Bodhidharma came to China and had a famous encounter with the emperor.
I don't know how he got an audience with the emperor either.
We have myths coexisting with historical reality in an interesting way.
When he met with the emperor, it was very much in line with what Jeff was reminding us about identity: that we can't really see identity.
We can see the sort of results of identity.
One of the results of identity is a powerful desire for approval and affirmation.
The people that we like are the ones that give us this.
Then the reverse.
Then we have the special challenge of having families where we're sort of stuck with them and they may or may not give us this, or they give it in different ways.
The emperor seems to be in a way standing in for this idea of identity in this encounter.
The emperor was a very good Zen student, very good Buddhist.
Buddhism had been in China for several hundred years, so it's a bit of a Zen recasting to say, then Buddhism started.
So the emperor described what he'd done.
He asked Bodhidharma, I have endowed temples and authorized ordinations, supported many, many monks and nuns, what is my merit?
You know this famous story probably.
What is my merit?
Do you approve of me?
And Bodhidharma said, no merit.
You've got to hand it to the emperor that he didn't say, off with his head, or something like that.
He was himself.
I think that the sort of surface meaning, the sort of kindergarten meaning, seems to be: super smart, wise monk, that's Zen, and kind of doddery emperor, and that's the other Buddhism.
But I don't think so.
I think they're telling us here that the emperor was in fact a very committed and realized practitioner, because he could recover from that.
Jeff was talking about that too.
Can you recover from it when somebody that you really esteem says to you, "You're no good.
No merit."
I'm not going to give you what your little self is wanting here.
So the emperor went on and asked about that.
What do you mean?
He said, "What is the first principle of the holy teaching?"
In other words, I thought it was this way.
Are you saying it some other way?
How does this work?
I want to get this right.
I don't want to fall in the hole again.
"What is the first principle of the holy teaching?"
And Bodhidharma said, "Vast emptiness.
Nothing holy."
Vast emptiness.
Nothing holy.
Nothing to hold onto.
Right?
So we can experience that in sesshin, right?
Moments come and go.
Breath comes and goes.
You lean into something a little bit.
You think you're kind of getting something.
Ouch!
Nothing holy.
Nothing to hold onto.
Or maybe the other way.
Oh!
My knee hurts.
Ow!
Breathe.
Oh!
I didn't have to hold onto that.
Nothing to hold onto.
But the emperor hung in there somehow.
And he asked, "Who are you?"
Or in this translation, "Who is this confronting me?"
Who am I talking to here?
And Bodhidharma said, "I don't know."
It's a very famous don't know. [unclear: "This thing lurches great"] so there are many different don't knows, actually.
So this is Bodhidharma's I don't know.
There are other kinds, but this is a very central and important one, and our typical don't know.
And then the story goes that he left the capital, Bodhidharma.
This was in the capital, Chang'an.
He found some semi-abandoned temple which had already been there for a long time.
I don't know what the monks who were there thought of him, but he went to some cave, maybe the cave behind the temple, and they just left him alone.
Keizan's story is that Buddha sat for six years, so Bodhidharma sat for nine years.
So we're just upping the ante.
Zen is better: nine years.
Famously he faced the wall in this cave and didn't move for nine years.
And there are all kinds of fabulous myths about Bodhidharma.
You probably know all this, but it's fun to bring it up at our Rohatsu celebration.
One is that he didn't want to fall asleep for those nine years, right?
He wanted to stay with his practice, so he rips his eyelids off.
And then he throws them on the ground, and the first tea plants sprout right there.
So he had tea to drink.
You heard that story, isn't that great?
There's lots more stuff like that.
But then after nine years along comes a worthy student named Weike.
This is our case for this weekend.
He actually had a dream, it turns out, that directed him to Bodhidharma.
And that's germane to Keizan too, because Keizan was famous for listening to his dreams, really paying attention to the teachings in his dreams.
So Weike had this dream to seek out this teacher behind Shaolin Temple, off in the mountain somewhere.
And Bodhidharma wouldn't let him in.
Of course it was the middle of winter, and the snow was coming down.
He was standing in the snow, but Bodhidharma just ignores him and continues practicing.
And finally, to prove his sincerity, he takes a sword.
I don't know why he would have a sword, but he takes a sword.
So maybe it was this sword behind me here.
And he cuts off his arm and says, "Your disciple's mind has no peace.
I beg you, master, please put it to rest.
My mind has no peace.
Please put it to rest."
And Bodhidharma said, "Bring me your mind and I will put it to rest."
And like Jeff said, these are very fluid about time.
This could have happened in ten minutes or ten years.
We don't know.
But at some point he replied, "I searched for my mind and I cannot find it.
I can't find my mind."
Bodhidharma said, "I have put it to rest."
Your mind is at rest.
So maybe that's our task in sesshin: to investigate this habitual mind, this mind that we think we have, this identity.

And maybe if we can shine some light, shine some awareness on that process that leads us so quickly away from contentment and into grasping or pushing away, maybe just by shining some light on it, it will naturally come to rest.
Because I don't think the implication here is that Bodhidharma had supernatural powers.
It's more that he in some way supported his student in looking at his life in a new way.
Tidily enough, later on Ueke grows up, becomes an important teacher, and along comes his disciple.
Of course, the way these stories are written, master and disciple recognize each other instantly.
And that actually does happen.
It actually does happen.
It's very tidy in these stories, though.
Great.
So along comes his student, whom we know as Senkan, and he basically asks him the exact same question.
Very tidy, huh?
Senkan, it turned out, also had some sort of vision.
Or actually his teacher had a vision, that's right.
Senkan's teacher had a vision that he should go to Ueke.
And it had to do with some bumps on his head, and it's all very esoteric.
But anyway, eventually Senkan, yeah, there were these special bumps on his head and that's how he knew.
So Senkan comes up to Ueke, as now Ueke's the Zen master and he's the student, right?
And he said, "I'm riddled with sickness.
I'm riddled with sickness."
One translation said he had leprosy.
"I'm riddled with sickness.
Please absolve me of my wrongdoing.
Absolve me of my wrongdoing."
So the idea is that his unskillful actions had generated negative karma and that's why he was sick, which is one of the reasons why you could get sick.
That was before there was so much biology confusing our spiritual understanding.
And Ueke made more or less the same reply that his teacher had made to him many years ago.
He said, "Bring me your wrongdoing.
Bring me your wrongdoing and I will cleanse you."
And Keizan writes that after a long pause Senkan said, "When I look for my wrongdoing I cannot find it."
And Ueke replied, "I have purified you.
You should now live by the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
In other words, you should join our monastery.
That's what living by Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha means.
One of the things that I appreciate most about these stories, as quirky as they are, which I think is helpful in a practical way for us, is this.
You get a majestic answer like that from a famous teacher: "I purified you.
You should now live by Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha."
Wouldn't you just be like, oh, thank you?
Even if you have no idea what he's saying.
But the students in these stories are willing to hang in there and ask, "Well, what do you mean by that?
I don't get it."
They're not embarrassed.
And actually that's the other thing that's been great for me about working with veterans at the Veterans Administration Hospital.
I say something a little bit cockamamie that doesn't make sense to them, and they're not so polite as you.
They have a great way of speaking.
They all speak this way.
I think they learned it in the army.
They kind of half raise their hand a little bit, because raising it all the way would be like kindergarten or something.
They lift up their hand a little bit and they say, "Excuse me.
I mean no disrespect, but."
And they go on and say that didn't make any sense, or what are you talking about.
I always say that: "I mean no disrespect."
And you're like, okay, here it comes.
It's really good training.
I recommend it.
Poor guys.
I don't mean to make fun of them.
They really suffer.
So anyway, same thing here.
Senkan, our student in our second story, our parallel story, says, "Well, I see that you are a monk and a member of the Sangha, but what do you mean by Buddha and Dharma?"
The teacher said live by Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.
So you're the Sangha, what's Buddha and Dharma?
And Huike said, "This mind is Buddha.
This mind is Dharma.
Dharma and Buddha are not separate."
And this is also true of Sangha.
So mind here doesn't mean the thinking apparatus.
It means something a little deeper.
It's the same word for mind and heart, so it's that word, mind-heart.
The sort of big mind.
The big mind is Buddha.
The big mind is Dharma.
And there's no difference.
They're not separate.
So this is a really important point for us.
Dharma and Buddha are not separate.
Dharma here means teachings on one level, and Buddha means awakening.
Right?
So back to our story of Buddha.
We tend to think, I'm following the teachings.
I'm heading in the direction of Buddha.
I know the story of Buddha.
I know what it looks like way over there.
But unfortunately I'm over here in a hole in the sidewalk.
So Huike's saying no, it's not that way.
Don't separate it like that.
It's going to cause suffering.
The practice is awakening.
And this of course was Dogen's central point too: Buddha and Dharma are not separate.
And yet we are suffering human beings.
We are confused.
We just sit for a day and we don't have to doubt our own confusion.
The teachings of Buddha went on to elaborate and explicate an enormous, complicated, sophisticated psychological analysis, sort of, of what's wrong with us.
There are many different lists of our mistaken attributes and our confusions, and there are very specific remedies explicated in the Buddhist canon.
And yet in the Zen school we don't deny that.
We don't deny that there's stuff that we should do.
You probably shouldn't just go about your life the same old way.
How's that working for you?
And yet not to be stuck on some sort of hamster wheel, you know?
Buddha's way over there.
We could do a new version of the poem where you get in a hamster wheel and just keep going: I'm not good enough, I'm going to try harder.
I'm not good enough, I'm going to try harder.
And so in some way it's kind of what Jeff was saying yesterday too, and in his talk when he was up here a few weeks ago: both are true.
This is like Suzuki Roshi's famous expression, you're all perfect just the way you are and you could use some improvement.
Right?
Our work here in sesshin is, can we soften up on this need to be one-dimensional?
If it's this way it can't be that way.
Right?
Maybe it's both and neither.
And anyway, to end our talk today I thought we might appreciate together a few verses of Senkan's famous poem, which Jeff also mentioned and which I know has been studied in Seattle.
So that's why I wanted to work on this: [unclear: "earlier Zen worthies kick all"] because Jeff a year ago was studying Bodhidharma, so it's his fault.
Senkan's famous poem is Xing Xing Ming, translated as Faith in Mind.
There are many different translations; this is just one I could grab on my computer.
*The great way is not difficult.
If only you do not pick and choose.
Neither love nor hate and you will clearly understand.
Be off by a hair and you will be as far apart as heaven from earth.
If you want it to appear be neither for or against.
For and against opposing each other is the mind's disease.
Without recognizing the mysterious principle it is useless to practice meditation.
The way is perfect like great space without lack, without excess.
But because of grasping and rejecting you cannot attain it.
Do not pursue conditioned existence do not abide in the acceptance of emptiness either.
In oneness and equality confusion vanishes of itself.
Stop activity and return to stillness.
And that stillness will be even more active.*
That's pretty interesting, huh?
The Buddha way, or we could say sesshin.
Let's say sesshin.
Sesshin is not difficult.
Let's start with that.
Sesshin is not difficult.
And it's not, actually.
Right?
And that's one of those one-dimensional axes, right?
Something's going to be either easy or hard, right?
But I think you've experienced it's both, right?
And neither.
It's just sesshin.
It's just your mind.
It's just breath.
So anyway, sesshin is not difficult.
*If only you do not pick and choose.
Neither love nor hate and you will clearly understand.
But be off by a hair and you are as far apart as heaven from earth.
If you want it to appear like awakening, if you want awakening to appear be neither for nor against.
For and against opposing each other is the mind's disease.
Without recognizing the mysterious principle, it is useless to practice meditation.
The way is perfect, like great space.
Without lack.
Without excess.
Because of grasping and rejecting you cannot attain it.
Because of grasping and rejecting you cannot attain it.
Do not pursue conditioned existence.
Do not abide in the acceptance of emptiness.
In oneness and equality confusion vanishes of itself.
Stop activity and return to stillness.
And that stillness will be even more active.*
Stillness will be active.
So, stop there.
I wish you a beautiful active stillness for the rest of our sesshin.
Oh, and I should make a few notes about tonight because people have been asking me how that might work.
I hope you haven't been too worried about it.
So, tonight the invitation is for heroic practice.
Sit all night, if you like.
What that means is we'll end the sesshin day just like usual.
We'll do the refuges.
The lights will be dim, the candles will be out, and we'll slip out of the room.
And a little bit later some of us who choose to will slip back in.
In fact, I have to go home and put my son to bed, so I'll be back in an hour or two probably.
When we come back in, if we want to, there'll be no bells, no candles.
It's kind of like secret practice almost.
We'll all face the wall.
We won't wear Rakusu or Okesa.
We won't even be us in that usual us-ness that we bring to things.
We'll just be Buddha.
We'll just be Bodhidharma.
We'll just be a blade of grass.
We'll just be the moon.
We'll just drift in.
We'll sit down.
Sit for as long as feels right for that not-us us.
I think I'll move the bowing mat out [unclear: "so that our face can be used"].
We can be intimate with the altar.
Don't worry about crossing in front, because Buddha doesn't even know you're here.
You don't have to worry about being judged by him or anybody else.
And so what I thought is, whenever you want to walk we can walk in the middle.
So there could be a more or less continuous kinhin happening, people coming and going from that, people coming and going from sitting.
